Oranges and Lemons

By: Joy Summers | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
It is almost the end of the orange harvest, and down on a farm deep in rural KZN on the banks of the Blaaukrantz river – the seeds of resilience were sown and now they have borne fruit. Against impo

Unique Selling Point:
A story that against the odds has a happy ending and subtly highlights woman empowerment in Women's month but without being in your face

Summary:
In November last year Carte Blanche brought you the story of the Sun Valley citrus estate. With its export quality oranges, this farm was the largest land redistribution project in the area between Weenen in the east, and the foothills of the Drakensburg in the west.

Investors managed the farm and exported the citrus. With a turnover of around R60 million, it could bring in profits of R10 million annually if it was managed well. But then in 2019 a violent war broke out between two community families who owned the farm. Forty people in the area were murdered. Management felt unsafe and one evening over a weekend, they packed up their assets under cover of darkness and drove their convoy of tractors and trailers, and fled, never to return. Nothing except an empty packhouse remained. There wasn’t even a chair left in the offices.

Carte Blanche arrived a few weeks later to find despair. There was no security, no money, and no formal management. The farm’s future hung in the balance and with it 700 people who depended on it to keep them from starvation. There was petty theft and the farm stood still. Without R12 million rand in emergency funding the farm would close.



Further information:
A FLICKER OF HOPE
There were, however, a few small flickering lights of hope. The police had brought in their heavies and confiscated 74 weapons including high-calibre rifles. The Induna’s had got involved and the families had signed a peace accord, so a semblance of peace was restored to this area that has always been plagued by violence.

Then came Roland Henderson a local beef farmer who knew the history of this project from his work, as a member of the local district land reform committee. He refused to let the farm die. First, he knocked on almost every government door he could think of to get funding, but all he got was moral support. Not even the land bank would assist.

Eventually he took his own savings and together with local businessman James Ncube, they took a leap of faith and invested. They now own 40% and the community own 60%.

“This takes a lot of faith to make this happen, and I didn’t always have the faith but there were many people who supported me and the farm and now we have light on the horizon’ says Roland.

JAMES NCUBE
James is a local businessman and he shares a vision with Roland. When it was clear there was no help coming from government he stepped up to the plate and put his money into the project. He also noticed five much needed tractors sitting at the Department of Agriculture doing nothing in Escort and organized to bring them to Sun Valley. It made the world of difference.

But the real difference came from the workers, the people Roland calls the bitter- einders. 120 people who came to work every day from November to March without salaries. They tended the trees and the vines and added crucial fertilizer to ensure that in 2020 there would be a harvest. In the packhouse three white managers who had run it previously were replaced by Vuthu, Baswepi and Sabatile who run the computers and keep it going. “This farm runs on woman power. I am very proud of that actually’, says Roland.

The office manager, Miss Mncube is a qualified teacher who used to pick fruit here in her youth. Roland is mentoring her to run the entire business one day. “She carries a lot of authority she has very good innate business sense and sees things very clearly. She is able to discipline men, she’s cautious because down here she’s a lady in a man’s world, but she is able to negotiate the business and the finance of it.” He says.

ESKOM, HAIL AND A FRAUDULENT PARTNER
But nothing about this has been plain sailing. Eskom switched off all the power points between Christmas and New Year and the man responsible then went on leave for two weeks. Hail went through the most promising orchards and one of their partners tried to defraud the operation even before it got off the ground.

But despite all these hurdles, they prevailed and this season they have just managed to pay R5million in salaries and export their harvest to Russia and the Middle East.

Many, many South African land reform projects end up on the scrap heap and Sun Valley almost did as well – but then just a handful of workers, commercial farmers and a businessman, chose another path with only faith and hope to guide them, and that has made all the difference.

FINAL SCRIPT SWEET HARVEST TX SUNDAY 23rd AUGUST 2020

Commentary One
In November last year I visited the Sun Valley Citrus Estate near Weenen, in KZN. The farm was on the brink of collapse. It was a sad and desolate place surrounded by violence.

Mpume Madondo CB 2019
The police here don’t help us. When you call them, they tell you directly we are scared of that place, that community.

Commentary Two
Conflict had ripped the community apart and criminals had murdered 40 people in the district. Terror reigned. Harvests rotted. Mpume Madondo worked at the farm

Mpume (CB November 2019)
What we do, is that at around 6pm we make sure everyone is inside sleeping, because once it gets dark it’s not safe. You hear gunshots and you don’t know who it is, or what is going on

Commentary Three
Eventually the police cracked down and confiscated 74 weapons, including high-calibre rifles. But it was too late for the Sun Valley farm. The investors who leased the communal land, fled over a weekend.

Phiweni Mncube grew up close to the farm, and she watched horrified, as they drove out the tractors and the trailers filled with the equipment that made the farm operational

Miss Mncube
I knew this farm is an important farm to everyone it was feeding a lot of families.

Commentary Four
She has studied management accounting and economics, and has been appointed to manage the Sun Valley office

Phiwene Mncube
My mum was working here. I went to university because of this farm, so I was crying

Commentary five
Roland Henderson is a local beef farmer and mentor on land reform projects. He’s watched as one land progamme after another has failed in this district, and he didn’t want to see that happen again, at Sun Valley.

Roland
I had an option that I could have commiserated with everybody and then turned around and gone home to be a beef farmer which is easier than this.


Commentary Six
But he didn’t, instead he made a decision that he would do whatever he could, to save the largest employer in the Inkosi Langabaleli district.

Roland
The communities had the option that they could have stripped the farm and none of us took those worst- case options

Commentary Seven
The local Induna’s had also signed a peace agreement to end the violence. But it was the bitter-einders, says Roland Henderson, who can take the credit for this unfolding story.

Roland
So, the people who invested the most in this farm are the staff who came to work that didn’t get a full salary

Commentary Eight
120 people, mostly women believed they could save the farm, even if it meant coming to work on an empty stomach. Sabathile Sithole is in charge of the packhouse

Sabathile Sithole
The reason why we are, where we are now, it’s because we were not working for the money, we were all working to develop the farm

Commentary Nine
And that meant developing the local people to replace the white managers who had left. Sabathile had a bit of computer experience, but she was initially nervous to run the packhouse

Sabathile
It was a big job and when they took me from printing the labels, to be the packhouse manager, I was like guys I won’t have power to run the packhouse….. and they give me that support

Commentary ten
Phiweni Mncube was selected for her grasp of numbers, her innate business sense, and her ability to manage relationships in a complicated social environment. There is no precedent of a woman leading a business operation of this scale in the area, and some men don’t easily take instruction.

Phiweni
It’s difficult, but I am trying, because some would say ag what can she tell us?

Roland
And we found that together marshalling our resources and management capabilities, we were able to replace that white management that had left and thereby empower the people to do what they knew how to do anyway, so at this point all the management has been taken care of by black people, and predominately ladies.

Commentary eleven
By the time I left the farm last year, Roland Henderson was already knocking on the doors of government and banks to get bridging finance of R12 million, or the farm would close.

Roland
And we knocked on many, many, doors, and the weeks went by and the months went by and then we realized it was never going to, and we would have to make do with what we had

Commentary twelve
But what they had was not even close to the R12 million they needed.

Roland
There were many times I lost faith, and when you feel your cause is worthwhile, and people turn you down, you do lose faith.

Commentary thirteen
So, Henderson dug into his own pocket and found a partner. Local businessman James Mbongwa

Roland
He is a teacher by profession and an engineer, and I heard that he was open to coercion to help us on this farm. In terms of the money James has invested the most of it, and he is a pretty firm disciplinarian

Commentary fourteen
But the obstacles in their way, were almost insurmountable. First Eskom cut off their power

Roland
So, Eskom in their wisdom switched off the electricity between Christmas and new year and then the gentleman that did that went on two weeks leave

Commentary fifteen
With no electricity and no money to pay Eskom, they couldn’t irrigate, and no water meant a reduced harvest

Phiweni
When there was no irrigation in the orchard, that was so terrible!

Commentary sixteen
Then the hail came. But God also came to the rescue and brought the rains



Roland
literally every three weeks that our trees needed rain we got rain, and we got it right into April. We had specialists look at our trees, and they said you guys have irrigated well and we said no we have not irrigated at all

Commentary seventeen
By January their first lemons were ready, and the oranges were ripening, but they still had no tractors or trailers

Phiweni
Huh, it was so terrible! I was thinking the picking season was coming but how are we going to fetch the oranges from the orchard.

Commentary eighteen
That problem was solved by Thenjiswa Gayi, an official from the department of agriculture, who loaned them 6 tractors for the harvest

Roland
Even though it’s a small amount of assistance, it was critical and Thenjiswa has been one of those agriculture officials who has gone beyond her calling to assist us.

Commentary nineteen
Sabatile Sithole recalls those dark days of no salaries, no working packhouse and only the experience of the older women to guide them through

Sabatile
It was the time we were harvesting the lemons. Hey! We were using containers, we used to polish the lemons with a cloth, sizing them with our eyes. There were old ladies here who were having experience, they are sizing using their eyes, packing it in the boxes, waxing it using the spray…Yoh laughs

Commentary twenty
Finally, they had harvested enough lemons to fill a container for export. Perhaps they could now pay wages. But those first lemons blighted their enthusiasm.

Phiweni Mncube
We wanted to export, but they all failed all the pallets and then I said ag, this thing can’t go anywhere!

Commentary twenty- one
Their post- harvest chemical mixture for the lemons was wrong and they rotted.

Roland
We learnt about things called sour rot which I had never heard of before as a beef farmer
Sabatile
So, we had to unpack them all and start again.
Roland
And those were our steep learning curves, those were the school fees that we paid.

Commentary twenty- two
They never made that mistake again. Then a bonus. Their helpful agent paid them in advance, for their next batch of lemons.

Phiweni
There was this little bit that we received and that gave us hope that one day, we’d get something more, something big.
It was giving us a little hope, that one day we will get something more, something big

Commentary twenty- three
Eventually in April, during lockdown, the sun rose once again in their valley. The orange harvest was about to begin

MUSIC UP SOUND

Roland
When we started it was daunting, I had never picked an orange in my life. But we are now looking forward to the next year because we now know that we can do this properly – we have taught ourselves those skills and we have coalesced into a cohesive business plan

Commentary twenty-four
By September when the harvest is complete, they will have exported over 100 000 boxes to the middle East. Fortunately, the ports stayed open during lockdown for citrus exports.

Sabathile
and it was magic because within a very short space of time things happened. We made history in one year.

Commentary Twenty- five
And the fearful Mpumi Madondo that I spoke to last year has been transformed by their efforts

Mpumi Madondo
And it shows that next year we will do more. We didn’t spray, we didn’t irrigate we didn’t do nothing and yet we are exporting!

Phiwene
and we have paid more or less R6 million in wages yoh -I am so proud of it.

Commentary twenty-six
By the end of the harvest they will have broken even and paid off all their debts. They still need tractors and equipment–but those will come. And it was only through their own faith and herculean efforts that the people of this valley have overcome violence and given themselves a future
Phumi
What I can say is that working together, our mutual understanding, that what we are doing is not for money, we are doing it for our children and our grandchildren and great-grandchildren. This is something big that we will never forget in our lives, even if we are 90 years old.

THE END


PROMO ONE
We revisit a citrus estate in Kwazulu Natal that had been besieged by violence, and discover how the local community have changed their fortunes through determination, and sacrifice


PROMO TWO
The Sun Valley Citrus Estate was on the brink of collapse last November. Nine months later it is exporting thousands of boxes of oranges. How did the farms fortunes change?


PROMO THREE
The orange harvest is almost over, and for a community of emerging farmers down in Kwa Zulu Natal its been an unbelievable year. How did they transform their failing farm

Commentary Twenty- five And the fearful Mpumi Madondo that I spoke to last year has been transformed by their efforts Mpumi Madondo And it shows that next year we will do more. We didn’t spray, we didn’t irrigate we didn’t do nothing and yet we are exporting! Phiwene and we have paid more or less R6 million in wages yoh -I am so proud of it. Commentary twenty-six By the end of the harvest they will have broken even and paid off all their debts. They still need tractors and equipment–but those will come. And it was only through their own faith and herculean efforts that the people of this valley have overcome violence and given themselves a future Phumi What I can say is that working together, our mutual understanding, that what we are doing is not for money, we are doing it for our children and our grandchildren and great-grandchildren. This is something big that we will never forget in our lives, even if we are 90 years old. THE END PROMO ONE We revisit a citrus estate in Kwazulu Natal that had been besieged by violence, and discover how the local community have changed their fortunes through determination, and sacrifice PROMO TWO The Sun Valley Citrus Estate was on the brink of collapse last November. Nine months later it is exporting thousands of boxes of oranges. How did the farms fortunes change? metadata.Unique Selling Point: A story that against the odds has a happy ending and subtly highlights woman empowerment in Women's month but without being in your face
metadata.Summary: In November last year Carte Blanche brought you the story of the Sun Valley citrus estate. With its export quality oranges, this farm was the largest land redistribution project in the area between Weenen in the east, and the foothills of the Drakensburg in the west. Investors managed the farm and exported the citrus. With a turnover of around R60 million, it could bring in profits of R10 million annually if it was managed well. But then in 2019 a violent war broke out between two community families who owned the farm. Forty people in the area were murdered. Management felt unsafe and one evening over a weekend, they packed up their assets under cover of darkness and drove their convoy of tractors and trailers, and fled, never to return. Nothing except an empty packhouse remained. There wasn’t even a chair left in the offices. Carte Blanche arrived a few weeks later to find despair. There was no security, no money, and no formal management. The farm’s future hung in the balance and with it 700 people who depended on it to keep them from starvation. There was petty theft and the farm stood still. Without R12 million rand in emergency funding the farm would close.
metadata.Further information: A FLICKER OF HOPE There were, however, a few small flickering lights of hope. The police had brought in their heavies and confiscated 74 weapons including high-calibre rifles. The Induna’s had got involved and the families had signed a peace accord, so a semblance of peace was restored to this area that has always been plagued by violence. Then came Roland Henderson a local beef farmer who knew the history of this project from his work, as a member of the local district land reform committee. He refused to let the farm die. First, he knocked on almost every government door he could think of to get funding, but all he got was moral support. Not even the land bank would assist. Eventually he took his own savings and together with local businessman James Ncube, they took a leap of faith and invested. They now own 40% and the community own 60%. “This takes a lot of faith to make this happen, and I didn’t always have the faith but there were many people who supported me and the farm and now we have light on the horizon’ says Roland. JAMES NCUBE James is a local businessman and he shares a vision with Roland. When it was clear there was no help coming from government he stepped up to the plate and put his money into the project. He also noticed five much needed tractors sitting at the Department of Agriculture doing nothing in Escort and organized to bring them to Sun Valley. It made the world of difference. But the real difference came from the workers, the people Roland calls the bitter- einders. 120 people who came to work every day from November to March without salaries. They tended the trees and the vines and added crucial fertilizer to ensure that in 2020 there would be a harvest. In the packhouse three white managers who had run it previously were replaced by Vuthu, Baswepi and Sabatile who run the computers and keep it going. “This farm runs on woman power. I am very proud of that actually’, says Roland. The office manager, Miss Mncube is a qualified teacher who used to pick fruit here in her youth. Roland is mentoring her to run the entire business one day. “She carries a lot of authority she has very good innate business sense and sees things very clearly. She is able to discipline men, she’s cautious because down here she’s a lady in a man’s world, but she is able to negotiate the business and the finance of it.” He says. ESKOM, HAIL AND A FRAUDULENT PARTNER But nothing about this has been plain sailing. Eskom switched off all the power points between Christmas and New Year and the man responsible then went on leave for two weeks. Hail went through the most promising orchards and one of their partners tried to defraud the operation even before it got off the ground. But despite all these hurdles, they prevailed and this season they have just managed to pay R5million in salaries and export their harvest to Russia and the Middle East. Many, many South African land reform projects end up on the scrap heap and Sun Valley almost did as well – but then just a handful of workers, commercial farmers and a businessman, chose another path with only faith and hope to guide them, and that has made all the difference.
